article_title: Improving EFL Learners' Pronunciation of English through Quiz-Demonstration-Practice-Revision (QDPR)
citation: Moedjito. (2017). Improving EFL Learners' Pronunciation of English through Quiz-Demonstration-Practice-Revision (QDPR). English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p10
title: Quiz-Demonstration-Practice-Revision (QDPR) learning model for pronunciation teaching
description: QDPR is a four-step pronunciation instruction model: Quiz (diagnosing difficulties via flashcards), Demonstration (explaining production in students' L1 while demonstrating), Practice (sound-spelling analysis in small groups plus oral practice), and Revision (remediation individually, in group, or classically). The article states "The medium of teachers' explanation in Bahasa Indonesia was the most prominent characteristic of QDPR learning model." It was designed to pursue global intelligibility for Indonesian EFL learners.
requirements: Teachers must be able to explain phoneme production in the students' L1 or a familiar language
Flashcards of the target phonemes, student worksheets, laptop and LCD projector are the recommended media
Student teachers attended an upgrading class on pronunciation instruction through QDPR before implementation
constraints: Evaluated only with learners sharing one linguistic background (Bahasa Sasak speakers) and only on phonemes identified as common and serious mispronunciations
target_learners: Indonesian university EFL students at second-semester level with diagnosed pronunciation difficulties
target_learning_goals: Ability to pronounce target English phonemes
examples: In the study, 11 student teachers taught 31 student participants with QDPR across 11 sessions covering 15 target phonemes such as /iː/, /ɪ/, /f/, /v/, /θ/ and /ð/.
key_sources: Moedjito. (2017). Improving EFL Learners' Pronunciation of English through Quiz-Demonstration-Practice-Revision (QDPR). English Language Teaching, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n1p10

article_title: 'It's fundamental': Quantum dot blinking experiment to teach critical thinking
citation: Laszlo Frazer, Heather F. Higginbotham, Toby D. M. Bell, and Alison M. Funston. (2020). 'It's fundamental': Quantum dot blinking experiment to teach critical thinking. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05223
title: Single quantum dot blinking laboratory experiment with wide-field fluorescence microscope and analysis software
description: A laboratory activity in which students spin-coat CdSe or CdSe/CdS/ZnS quantum dots onto coverslips and record 100-second, 10 frame-per-second videos of luminescence on an inverted wide-field microscope with a 488 nm laser and EMCCD camera, "allowing about ﬁve students to complete the experiment per hour". A custom menu-and-dialogue package generates photon trajectories, off-time histograms, and power law exponents via log transformation and Poisson weighted linear regression. Blinking is visible to the dark-adjusted eye through the eyepieces.
requirements: A large numerical aperture objective is essential to ensure efficient light collection
Students must choose a sufficiently low quantum dot concentration to achieve single-particle measurements
constraints: Lower cost adaptations are possible; core-shell quantum dots are significantly easier to measure due to generally higher quantum yields
Quantum dots may be toxic and lasers may cause eye injury
target_learners: advanced undergraduate, masters, and first-year doctoral students
target_learning_goals: understanding stochastic processes and power law distributions
examples: Students prepared one solution each, selected particles and background pixels, set a brightness threshold, and selected a histogram domain before fitting the exponent
key_sources: Laszlo Frazer, Heather F. Higginbotham, Toby D. M. Bell, and Alison M. Funston. (2020). 'It's fundamental': Quantum dot blinking experiment to teach critical thinking. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.05223
